label: lem:world
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:world}
Let $x$ and $y$ be incomparable in $P$, let $P_1=P+xy$ and $P_2=P+yx$ be
the two possible outcomes of comparing them, and fix
$L\in\mathcal{D}_{i-1}(P)$.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item If both $x$ and $y$ lie in $L$, the weight is unchanged in both
  outcomes: $\psi_L(P_1)=\psi_L(P_2)=\psi_L(P)$.
  \item If exactly one of them lies in $L$, one outcome keeps the weight
  $\psi_L(P)$ and the other sets it to $0$.
  \item If neither lies in $L$, the two outcomes together keep at least the
  weight: $\psi_L(P_1)+\psi_L(P_2)\ge\psi_L(P)$.
\end{enumerate}
The same holds for an initial set $A\in\mathcal{D}_i(P)$ with weight $2^{a(A)}$,
with inside and outside exchanged: the weight is unchanged if $x,y\notin A$,
one outcome keeps it if exactly one of them lies in $A$, and the two
outcomes together keep at least the weight if $x,y\in A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Adding $x<y$ creates only relations $u<v$ with $u\le x$ and $y\le v$. Let
$M=\Omega\setminus L$. If $x\in L$, every $u\le x$ lies in $L$, so no
relation inside $M$ and none from $M$ into $L$ is created; this gives the
first case and the surviving outcome of the second. The outcome placing an
element of $M$ below one of $L$ destroys $L$ as a down-set. If $x,y\in M$,
then $L$ stays a down-set in both outcomes, and a minimal $v$ of $M$ can
gain a predecessor in $M$ only through $y\le v$, which forces $v=y$. So
$b(L)$ drops by at most one in each child, and
$\psi_L(P_1)+\psi_L(P_2)\ge2\cdot2^{b(L)-1}$. Order reversal gives the
statement for $A$.
head: environment

label: thm:phi
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Removing comparisons with known outcomes does not increase the number of
leaves, and at a correct leaf the problem is solved, where
$\mathrm{FG}=\mathrm{FG}^{\delta}=|C|=1$ and $\Phi^*=1$. It therefore suffices to show
$\Phi^*(P)\le\Phi^*(P_1)+\Phi^*(P_2)$ for incomparable $x,y$, and to sum
this inequality over the tree. Write $\Delta F=F(P_1)+F(P_2)-F(P)$.
Every compatible solution survives in at least one child, the children's
solutions are solutions of $P$, and a solution survives in both exactly
when $x$ and $y$ lie on the same side of its answer. Hence
\[
 \Delta|C|=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{D}_{i-1}(P),\ x,y\in L}(b(L)+1)
          +\sum_{A\in\mathcal{D}_i(P),\ x,y\notin A}(a(A)+1).
\]
Down-sets of the children are down-sets of $P$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:world}, every $L$ contributes at least $0$ to $\Delta\mathrm{FG}$,
and $L$ with $x,y\in L$ contributes exactly $2^{b(L)}$; likewise for
$\Delta\mathrm{FG}^{\delta}$ and $A$ with $x,y\notin A$. Therefore
\[
 \Delta\Phi^*\ge\sum_{x,y\in L}\bigl(2^{b(L)}-b(L)-1\bigr)
   +\sum_{x,y\notin A}\bigl(2^{a(A)}-a(A)-1\bigr)\ge0,
\]
since $2^t\ge t+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is the classical argument about crucial
comparisons~\cite[Sec.~5.3.3]{knuth}, \cite{fg}, applied along one total
order. Answer all comparisons according to a total order extending $P$ that
lists $L$, then $e$, then $U$; let $A=L\cup\{e\}$ and $M=\Omega\setminus L$.
A new relation inside $A$ requires a comparison with both ends in $A$, since
$A$ is an initial segment of that order, and such a comparison removes at
most one maximal element of $A$. Dually, only comparisons inside $M$ remove
minimal elements of $M$, at most one each. At the end $e$ must be the only
maximal element of $A$ and the only minimal element of $M$, which needs at
least $a_s$ and $b_s$ comparisons respectively. As $A\cap M=\{e\}$, no
comparison is counted twice.
head: environment

label: cor:combined
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:combined}
$V_i(P)\ge\mathrm{LB}(P)=\max\{\lceil\log_2\Phi^*(P)\rceil,\mathrm{KEY}(P)\}$.
Since $2^t\ge t+1$ gives $\mathrm{FG},\mathrm{FG}^{\delta}\ge|C|$, this is never weaker than the
compatible-solution bound or either one-sided weight bound.
head: environment

label: prop:phiopt
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:phiopt}
If $\Psi_{F,G}(E_n,1)\le2^{V_1(n)}$ and $\Psi_{F,G}(E_n,n)\le2^{V_n(n)}$ for
all $n\ge1$, then $F(t),G(t)\le2^t-t-1$ for all $t\ge0$, and hence
$\Psi_{F,G}\le\Phi^*$ on every problem.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the minimum of $E_n$ there is one lower set with $b=n-1$ and $n$
singleton initial sets with $a=0$, so $n+F(n-1)\le2^{n-1}$. The maximum
gives the bound for $G$. Substituting termwise gives $\Psi_{F,G}\le\Phi^*$.
head: environment

label: rem:leafcount
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:leafcount}
No lower bound on the number of leaves of every correct tree can prove
$V_8(16)\ge29$ by taking its ceiling logarithm. The 252-function
29-comparison certificate unfolds into a tree with 248,381,440 syntactic
leaves, fewer than $2^{28}$, computed by two independent counts. Any bound
valid for all correct trees is at most this number, so its ceiling
logarithm is at most 28. A proof of 29, if true, must use depth or path
information.
head: environment
name: A limit of leaf counting

title: Open problems
body_md:
Is $V_8(16)$ equal to 28 or 29? A 28-comparison certificate would settle it
constructively; a proof of 29 must exclude all such algorithms and, by
Remark~\ref{rem:leafcount}, needs more than a total leaf count. An analytic
proof of $V_7(16)\ge28$ would remove the dependence on a large computation.
The gaps for $n=17$ at ranks 6--9 remain open. Finally, can the runner-up
opening be extended into a family of good selection algorithms, for example
for central ranks of $2^k$ elements?
